# Decoding High HC and CO with Low NO and CO2 in Emission Tests

You are facing a classic stoichiometry puzzle that often trips up even seasoned mechanics: high Hydrocarbons (HC) and Carbon Monoxide (CO), paired with low Nitrogen Oxides (NO) and low Carbon Dioxide (CO2). Your data points—13.6% CO2, 0.1% O2, 333 ppm HC, and 2.00% CO—tell a specific story about the combustion chamber environment.

The most critical indicator here is the CO2 level at 13.6%. In a properly tuned gasoline engine operating near stoichiometry (the ideal air-fuel ratio), you should see CO2 values typically between 14.5% and 15.5%, depending on the fuel octane and spark timing. A reading of 13.6% signifies that the exhaust is not fully oxidized because there isn't enough oxygen present to convert all the carbon in the fuel into CO2. Instead, some carbon forms incomplete combustion products: Carbon Monoxide (CO) and unburned Hydrocarbons (HC).

The low O2 reading of 0.1% confirms that the engine is running slightly lean or at stoichiometry during the test cycle; the catalytic converter has consumed most of the available oxygen, but not enough to drive the reaction fully if fuel delivery is erratic. However, the elevated CO and HC suggest a fundamental issue with combustion efficiency rather than just an overly rich mixture. If this were a simple rich condition caused by a stuck injector, you would expect high O2 in the exhaust before the catalyst kicks in, and potentially higher NO due to excessive heat from extra fuel. The absence of high NO suggests the combustion temperature isn't spiking uncontrollably, which points away from severe misfires causing localized hot spots.

One primary suspect is compression loss in one or more cylinders. When cylinder pressure drops due to worn piston rings, valve guides, or head gasket issues, the air-fuel mixture cannot burn efficiently. This leads to unburned fuel exiting as HC and incomplete oxidation resulting in CO. The low NO makes sense here because a misfire often cools that specific cylinder locally, preventing the formation of nitrogen oxides which require high temperatures. To investigate this mechanically without tearing down the engine immediately, perform a compression test or a leak-down test. If you have access to an OBD-II scanner capable of live data logging, watch for uneven Cylinder Misfire Counts (P030X codes) during a road test that correlates with these emission spikes.

Another possibility involves excessive oil consumption via Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV). Burning oil creates HC and CO because the lubricating additives prevent proper combustion of the hydrocarbon chain. While this usually raises HC significantly, the impact on CO depends on how much fuel is being displaced by the oil-air mixture. If the crankcase pressure is high enough to blow past piston rings into the cylinder, you get a similar result to low compression: incomplete burn and higher HC/CO ratios. A simple visual check for blue smoke under acceleration can confirm this, though a smog tester cannot detect it directly.

Fuel delivery issues also play a role. A faulty Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor might be sending erratic signals that confuse the Engine Control Unit (ECU). If the ECU enriches the mixture intermittently to compensate for perceived low airflow, you get pockets of rich combustion (high HC/CO) mixed with lean pockets (low CO2). The inconsistency prevents the catalytic converter from maintaining a steady state. Verify MAF data by comparing voltage or frequency outputs against manufacturer specifications while idling and under load.

Finally, consider the condition of your oxygen sensors. You mentioned having a new sensor, but ensure it was installed correctly and that the wiring harness is free of damage. A failing upstream O2 sensor can cause the ECU to oscillate between open and closed loop, creating the exact mixture instability seen in your results. Before replacing parts again, rule out mechanical compression issues first, as they are the most common root cause for this specific HC/CO/NO pattern on an older BMW platform like the 325i E30.
